thread.title: How Much Stock Could Apple Have Repurchased In Fourth Quarter? - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Billy Duberstein
title: How Much Stock Could Apple Have Repurchased In Fourth Quarter? - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple's ( AAPL ) fourth quarter has been terrible for shareholders… or terrific, depending on your time horizon, and estimate of Apple's intrinsic value. If you are worried about the short term, it has been terrible, as the stock fell more than 30% since the start of CY Q4.
However, if you think that Apple's intrinsic value is higher than current prices - or far higher, the current swoon has been a huge opportunity for the company to retire shares at a discount.
Thanks to last year's tax reform measures, large tech companies with overseas cash have been able to repatriate that cash at lower rates. No company had as much cash overseas as Apple, with more than $130 billion net of its debt (which was taken on in very low rates).
As you can see (above), Apple's market price has declined precipitously with the market swoon. Since Apple was still a buyer of its stock back in CY Q3 with the stock in the $220s - the company repurchased about $19.1 billion in the September quarter - how much could the company have purchased during the recent market action? Could Apple have turned on the spigots and gotten to net cash neutral?
AAPL data by YCharts
The rules for companies buying their own stock Companies can repurchase their own stock at will, but with some restrictions. These restrictions are:
Larger companies cannot repurchases shares in the last 10 minutes of trading. Smaller companies (under $1 million volume per day) can't buy within the last 30 minutes of trading. Companies also are not supposed to buy close to quarter-end through 48 hours after an earnings release (because they know things investors don't). However - companies are allowed to buy shares through a financial institution that does programmatic buying, not controlled by the company in question (called Rule 10b5-1). Companies cannot repurchase more than 25% of the average trading volume over the previous four weeks. So, what could have Apple done in Q4? For a maximum allocation, I'll look to point 4 - the 25% of average trading volume. This is assuming that during discretionary periods, Apple was as aggressive as possible, and during blackout periods, Apple implemented the highest possible amount of programmatic buying (also, December had very high levels of volume during the market rout, opening the door for above-average repurchases).
Today, Apple's 50-day average daily volume was 44.41 million shares, according to Nasdaq data. I'll use this number for the whole quarter since October and December were quite volatile (though it may have been a bit less since this figure includes all of December).
For the sake of argument, let's assume that Apple thinks its stock is crazily undervalued and purchased the maximum possible amount of stock in the quarter.
So, that would lead to 11.1 million shares per day. If we multiply that by 64 trading days in the quarter, we get 710.4 million shares . What does that equal? At an average price of about $193 per share, it equals about $137.1 billion - almost exactly the amount of net cash Apple had on its balance sheet. If Apple bought that much, it would amount to about 15% of shares outstanding - in one quarter.
Now, do I think Apple bought back that much? Probably not. That would be about seven times the amount of shares purchased last quarter, and only if Apple went "full throttle" on share repurchases amid a very volatile and uncertain investing and macro environment.
However, I'll be disappointed for sure if the company did not buy back a significant amount of shares in the quarter and far more than the $19 billion in Q3. If Apple didn't repurchase more than $20 billion in the quarter, analysts should ask a lot of questions. I personally expect that Apple has opened up the spigots and will be watching this figure in the FY Q1 earnings report.
